reader.title: Newport mob threat (1903)
bases: A mob threatened the village after a death and about 25 Black men left for the night; no killing, injury or property damage is reported (A2).
The only account is one Newport correspondent's column in the St. Louis Palladium (A2); no other paper, Black or white, was found reporting it.

summary.text: The Newport mob threat of 1903 was a threat by a "revenging mob" against the village of Newport on the Monday night after a death in a Black-run "joint" there in late September 1903.
About 25 Black men left the village for the night, and no violence was reported.
The only account came from the St. Louis Palladium's Newport correspondent, who used it to campaign against the joint.
Newport was a village within daily boat travel of St. Louis, where some Black parents sent their children to school at ten cents a day.
Its school answered to "the Madison board of education," and local disputes went to court in Edwardsville.
The Palladium's Newport writer, allied with a "Booker Washington league," campaigned against a "dive of beer slushers" near G. W. Young's store.
Two weeks before the threat, the column already quoted a resident's excuse for siding with "the mob": "I am afraid my house may be set afire."
According to the correspondent, a death occurred in a "notorious Colored 'joint'" in Newport on "Sunday night, September 26"; the column named neither the dead person nor anyone accused.
On the following Monday night Newport "was threatened by a revenging mob," and about 25 Black men left the village until morning.
No report of arrests, an inquest or further violence appears in the coverage.

The correspondent warned that residents who sided with the joint's operator would "yet see the white man mob in that dive," a Black man burned alive in the streets and homes burned, unless they helped the league close it.
A week later the column blamed the village's troubles in part on "the vote-seeking, common, white element" that encouraged its "corrupt element."
The episode is known from a few lines in the Palladium's Newport column of October 10, 1903, among notices about a new pay school.
Rather than treating the threat as a crime by the mob, the writer presented it as the consequence of tolerating the joint and as a warning to Black residents.
No report of the death or the threat was found in the white press.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Newport column)
accounts.gist: After a death in a Colored 'joint' on Sunday night, September 26, a revenging mob threatened Newport the next Monday night and about 25 Negro men left the village for the night.

framing.detail: The Palladium's Newport writer did not condemn the mob directly but used the threat to attack the 'joint' and its supporters, warning they 'will yet see the white man mob in that dive'.

record_check.dossier: Not stated; columns mention a Madison board of education, a court case in Edwardsville and boat travel to St. Louis. Research's suggestion of Missouri rests only on a quoted Missouri school statistic and is not supported.
Consistent: the threat came 'the following Monday night' after a death on 'Sunday night, September 26' (Sept. 26, 1903 fell on a Saturday; either reading puts the Monday on Sept. 28).
Black: the men who left were 'Negro men'.
About 25 unnamed Black men who fled for the night.

info: Death in the 'joint' on 'Sunday night, September 26'; mob threat 'the following Monday night'
Newport, a village whose Black children were sent to St. Louis school by boat; its school answered to a Madison board of education and a local case was tried in Edwardsville
About 25 Black ('Negro') men who left the village for the night; no one named
None stated; the mob is called 'revenging' after a death in a 'notorious Colored "joint"'; the dead person and any accused are not named
A 'revenging mob', otherwise unidentified; race not stated for the Monday-night mob

sources.note: Newport column before the death: churches, school, boat fare to St. Louis, the 'joint' near G. W. Young's, a resident who 'hold[s] with the mob' for fear of arson.
quotes: I am afraid my house may be set afire, the reason I hold with the mob.
